title: Earth's next ice age may have already begun. Global warming stopped it
summary: Scientists have uncovered surprising evidence that Earth’s next ice age may have already begun, only to be stopped by global warming. By studying ancient plants preserved beneath the Barnes Ice Cap in the Canadian Arctic, researchers discovered that the remnants of a massive ice sheet began expanding again about 2,000 years ago, signaling the possible start of a new glacial period. But by the 1960s, rising temperatures had reversed that growth, causing the ice to shrink instead.

Credit: Shutterstock About 2,000 years ago, the remnants of a massive ice sheet in the Canadian Arctic began expanding once again. According to new research, this slow buildup of ice may have marked the beginning of Earth's next glacial period, commonly called an ice age. But something unexpected happened. By the 1960s, rising summer temperatures had reversed the trend, causing the ice to retreat instead of grow. The findings suggest that global warming may have interrupted a new ice age that was already getting underway, fundamentally altering a natural climate cycle that has shaped Earth for millions of years. "It was just getting started, everything was normal, the next glaciation was about to happen -- and yet it stopped," says Nicolás Young, a geochemist at Columbia Climate School's Lamont-Doherty Earth Observatory. "It's a very powerful example of how we have jolted the system." Ancient Arctic Ice Reveals a Surprising Climate History In a study published in Science , Young and fellow Lamont geochemist Joerg Schaefer, along with their colleagues, investigated the history of the Laurentide Ice Sheet. This enormous mass of ice covered much of Canada and the northern United States between approximately 95,000 and 20,000 years ago. At its greatest extent, the Laurentide stretched from north of the Arctic Circle all the way south to Illinois. In some locations, its ice was more than two miles thick. Although most of this enormous ice sheet disappeared as the climate warmed, one surviving piece remains. Known as the Barnes Ice Cap, this ancient remnant sits on central Baffin Island in Nunavut, Canada, and covers an area roughly the size of Delaware. "People always say that it disappeared, but that's not true," says Young. Scientists already knew that the Laurentide Ice Sheet had repeatedly grown and retreated during the roughly 2.6 million years since extensive continental glaciation began in North America. What remained uncertain was whether the ice sheet had ever become smaller than it is today before expanding again. Answering that question could reveal whether a new cycle of glaciation had begun much more recently than scientists previously believed. (A note on terminology: Technically, we are still living in an ice age-the Late Cenozoic Ice Age-which started about 34 million years ago. Within it, colder glacial periods alternate with warmer interglacial ones, including the one we live in now. What people casually call an "ice age" is usually a glacial period. The last glacial period ended about 11,700 years ago.) Ancient Plants Preserved Beneath Ice Hold the Clues Piecing together the history of an ice sheet is particularly challenging when researchers are looking for evidence of its smallest extent and earliest stages of regrowth. As glaciers advance, they frequently scrape across the land, destroying the geological traces that could reveal where and when the ice first began spreading. The Barnes Ice Cap, however, offers an unusual opportunity to investigate this history. Unlike most glaciers, it is frozen directly to the bedrock beneath it and does not slide across the landscape. As a result, plants that once grew in areas later covered by expanding ice can remain preserved in place for thousands of years. Since the Barnes Ice Cap began retreating in 1960, previously buried vegetation has gradually emerged from beneath the melting ice. Researchers can collect these ancient plant remains and determine when they were alive using radiocarbon dating. This technique measures carbon-14, a harmlessly radioactive form of carbon that living organisms absorb from the atmosphere. Once an organism dies, its carbon-14 begins breaking down at a predictable rate. By measuring how much remains, scientists can estimate when the plant stopped growing and became buried beneath the ice. These dates provide a record of when the advancing glacier covered different parts of the landscape. "If you do this enough times, you can actually develop a timeline of that ice margin systematically advancing over plants. You're actually tracking the expansion of that ice margin," says Young. Earth's Next Ice Age May Have Begun 2,000 Years Ago The research team examined ancient vegetation uncovered by the retreating Barnes Ice Cap, along with plant remains exposed beneath smaller ice caps that have recently melted in the surrounding region. Together, these samples allowed the scientists to reconstruct thousands of years of glacial change. Their results indicate that the Laurentide Ice Sheet reached its smallest extent approximately 3,000 years ago. Then, around 2,000 years ago, temperatures became cold enough for the remaining ice to begin expanding again.
